facts.statement: Oxalaia fossils were discovered in 1999 on Cajual Island within the Alcântara Formation.

facts.statement: Oxalaia quilombensis is the largest carnivorous dinosaur discovered in Brazil.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Oxalaia is a distinct genus or a junior synonym of Spinosaurus.

facts.statement: Oxalaia is known from two partial skull bones that possess two replacement teeth per socket and a sculptured secondary palate.

facts.statement: Oxalaia lived in a tropical, heavily forested habitat surrounded by an arid landscape.

facts.statement: Oxalaia had a partly piscivorous lifestyle similar to modern crocodilians.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence suggests spinosaurids like Oxalaia also preyed on small dinosaurs and pterosaurs.

facts.statement: Oxalaia fossils were recovered from the Laje do Coringa locality in 1999.

facts.statement: The discovery of Oxalaia was accidental, as noted by paleontologist Elaine Machado.
facts.quote: Palaeontologist Elaine Machado, of the National Museum of Rio de Janeiro, was surprised to find such a well-preserved fossil at the site and stated in a press release that "this is how most scientific discoveries happen, it was by accident".

facts.statement: The holotype specimen MN 6117-V consists of fused premaxillae from a large individual found in situ.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen of Oxalaia quilombensis, designated MN 6117-V, was found in situ (at its original place of deposition) with part of the left side embedded in the rock matrix; it consists of the fused premaxillae (frontmost snout bones) from a large individual.

facts.statement: An isolated left maxilla fragment (MN 6119-V) was referred to Oxalaia due to shared spinosaurid traits.
facts.quote: An isolated and incomplete left maxilla (main upper jaw bone) fragment (MN 6119-V) was referred to Oxalaia because it showed the same general traits occurring in spinosaurids

facts.statement: The Oxalaia bone fragments were housed at the National Museum of Rio de Janeiro.
facts.quote: Both bone fragments were found on Cajual Island, Maranhão, in the Northeast Region of Brazil, and were housed at the National Museum of Rio de Janeiro.

facts.statement: A fire in 2018 at the National Museum of Rio de Janeiro possibly destroyed the Oxalaia specimens.
facts.quote: In 2018, a fire engulfed the palace housing the museum, possibly destroying Oxalaias specimens, along with various other fossils found in Brazil.

facts.statement: In 2025, paleontologist Rubi Pêgas noted that badly damaged Oxalaia remains were recovered and a publication is in preparation.
facts.quote: It was noted by paleontologist Rubi Pêgas in 2025 that the badly damaged remains of Oxalaia were recovered, and the publication for the recovered items is in preparation.

facts.statement: Oxalaia was announced by the Brazilian Academy of Sciences in March 2011 alongside Pepesuchus and Brasiliguana.
facts.quote: The discoveries of Oxalaia and of the Late Cretaceous reptiles Pepesuchus and Brasiliguana were announced in a presentation by the Brazilian Academy of Sciences in March 2011.

facts.statement: Elaine Machado described Oxalaia as the dominant reptile of Cajual Island.
facts.quote: Machado described Oxalaia as "the dominant reptile of [what is now] Cajual Island".

facts.statement: Oxalaia was described by Alexander Kellner, Elaine Machado, Sergio Azevedo, Deise Henriques, and Luciana Carvalho.

facts.statement: The maxillae of Oxalaia display a pair of elongated, thin processes extending forward along the midline of the roof of the mouth.

facts.statement: The undersides of the premaxillae in Oxalaia are greatly ornamented, unlike the smoother condition found in other spinosaurids.

facts.statement: The premaxillae of Oxalaia possess seven tooth sockets on each side.

facts.statement: Unlike its Early Cretaceous relatives Suchomimus and Cristatusaurus, Oxalaia lacked serrations on its teeth.

facts.statement: Oxalaia had two replacement teeth in each socket alongside a single functional tooth, a feature Kellner notes is common in sharks or some reptiles but not theropods.

facts.statement: Cross-sections of Oxalaia's teeth show a typical oval shape found in spinosaurs, rather than the lateral compression seen in other theropod teeth.

facts.statement: Kellner and colleagues differentiated Oxalaia from other spinosaurids based on distinguishing craniodental features, including a sculptured palatal part of the premaxillae and two replacement teeth per position.
facts.quote: Kellner and colleagues differentiated Oxalaia from it and other spinosaurids by its autapomorphic (distinguishing) craniodental features, like its sculptured palatal part of the premaxillae, and the possession of two replacement teeth in each position.

facts.statement: In 2020, Robert Smyth and colleagues argued that the distinguishing features of Oxalaia quilombensis were insufficient for a separate taxon and were instead a result of individual variation.
facts.quote: In 2020, a paper by Robert Smyth and colleagues assessing spinosaurines from the Kem Kem Group did not find the autapomorphies of Oxalaia quilombensis sufficient to warrant a separate taxon, but instead considered them a result of individual variation.

facts.statement: Subsequent studies have rejected the synonymy of Oxalaia with Spinosaurus aegyptiacus based on diagnostic features found in the holotype and referred specimens.

facts.statement: As a spinosaurid, Oxalaia likely had large, robust forelimbs, relatively short hind limbs, elongated neural spines forming a crest or sail on its back, and high neural spines on its tail vertebrae that may have helped it swim like modern crocodiles.

facts.statement: Spinosaurids like Oxalaia likely spent most of their time near or in water, feeding mainly on aquatic animals to avoid direct competition with other large predators, though they could sustain themselves as terrestrial animals if necessary.

facts.statement: Oxalaia's conical, transversely oval teeth and nostrils, which were positioned further back in the skull than in most theropods, likely prevented water from entering its nasal passages while fishing.
facts.quote: Los dientes cónicos, transversalmente ovalados de Oxalaia y sus orificios nasales, que se retrajeron más atrás en el cráneo que en la mayoría de los terópodos, probablemente eviten que el agua entre en sus fosas nasales mientras pescan, son característicos de los espinosáuridos.
